items.title: Figure 14 caption question: A 140-N sign hangs from a ring. A horizontal cable pulls the ring to the right, and a second cable pulls it up and to the left at 40° above the horizontal. The ring is at rest. Compare the vertical component of the angled cable's pull with the weight of the sign, and find the tension in the angled cable.

question.html: Physics idea. The ring is in equilibrium, so the net force is zero in each direction separately. Work. Vertically, the only upward force on the ring is the vertical component of the angled pull, 𝑇sin40°, and the only downward force is the weight, 140 N. So
Horizontally, the angled cable's horizontal component 𝑇cos40° = 167 N (to the left) is balanced by the horizontal cable's pull to the right.

answer.html: The vertical component of the angled pull equals the weight (140 N, opposite direction). The angled cable's tension is 2.2 × 10<sup>2</sup> N, and the horizontal cable pulls with 167 N.

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3, p. 129): Two forces act on a post: 24 N toward the east and 45 N toward the north. Find the resultant and the equilibrant, and state how they are related.

question.html: Physics idea. The resultant is the vector sum. The equilibrant is the single force that makes the total zero. Work. The forces are perpendicular: 𝑅= √(24 N)<sup>2</sup> + (45 N)<sup>2</sup> = 51 N,
The equilibrant must cancel this, so it has the same magnitude, 51 N, pointing the opposite way: 62° south of west.

answer.html: Resultant 51 N at 62° north of east; equilibrant 51 N at 62° south of west. The equilibrant has the same magnitude and the opposite direction, so resultant plus equilibrant equals zero.

items.title: Text question (Inclined Planes): How does the component of a skier's weight perpendicular to the slope change as the slope angle increases?

question.html: Physics idea. The perpendicular component is 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑, where 𝜑 is the angle of the incline above horizontal. Work. For 0° < 𝜑< 90°, cos𝜑 decreases as 𝜑 increases. Examples: cos10° = 0.98, cos30° = 0.87, cos60° = 0.50.

answer.html: It gets smaller as the angle increases (equal to the full weight on a flat surface, zero on a vertical wall).

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3, p. 130): Why is it convenient to choose the y-axis perpendicular to the incline when solving a sliding problem?

answer.html: The object does not accelerate perpendicular to the surface, so ∑𝐹<sub>𝑦</sub>= 0 there, which gives 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑 directly. The normal force already lies along that axis, and only the weight has to be resolved.

items.title: Practice Problem 29 (Lesson 3): Draw a free-body diagram of a 55-g gecko climbing at steady speed up a smooth wall that is inclined 25.0° from vertical, and find the size of each force.

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 0.055 kg, the wall is 25.0° from vertical, so it is 65.0° above horizontal. Steady speed means zero net force. Physics idea. Three forces act: weight (straight down), normal force (perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from it), and friction (parallel to the surface, pointing up the slope). The gecko does not slip, so the friction is static (adhesion) friction. The weight components along and perpendicular to the surface are 𝑚𝑔sin65.0° and 𝑚𝑔cos65.0°, so 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑚𝑔sin65.0° and 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos65.0°. Work.

answer.html: The diagram shows 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 0.54 N down, 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 0.23 N perpendicular to the wall, and static friction 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 0.49 N up the wall. The sum of the three forces is zero. Check. On a steep surface the friction force is larger than the normal force (0.49 > 0.23), which is why the gecko needs a very large static friction coefficient (at least tan65.0° = 2.1).

items.title: Practice Problem 30 (Lesson 3): A 1.25-kg book rests on a tray tilted at 22.0°. Find the components of the book's weight parallel and perpendicular to the tray.

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 1.25 kg, 𝜑= 22.0°. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>∥</sub> and 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>⊥</sub>. Physics idea. Resolve the weight 𝑚𝑔 along and perpendicular to the plane: parallel = 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑, perpendicular = 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.
𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>∥</sub>= 𝑚𝑔sin22.0° = 4.59 N,

answer.html: Parallel component 4.59 N (down the slope); perpendicular component 11.4 N (into the tray) Check. √4.59<sup>2</sup> + 11.36<sup>2</sup> = 12.25 N, which equals 𝑚𝑔.

items.title: Practice Problem 31 (Lesson 3): A 36.5-kg child sits at rest on a playground slide inclined at 28.0°. What is the normal force the slide exerts on her?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 36.5 kg, 𝜑= 28.0°. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>. Physics idea. Perpendicular to the slide there is no acceleration, so 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> balances the perpendicular weight component: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.

answer.html: 316 N Check. It is less than her weight (358 N), as always on an incline.

items.title: Practice Problem 32 (Lesson 3, Challenge): At what incline angle is the component of an object's weight parallel to the surface equal to 0.80 times the component perpendicular to it?

question.html: Physics idea. Parallel = 𝑚𝑔sin𝜃, perpendicular = 𝑚𝑔cos𝜃. Work.

answer.html: 𝜃= 39° (38.7° before rounding) Check. At 45° the two are equal, so a slightly smaller angle is right for a parallel part that is slightly smaller.

items.title: Practice Problem 33 (Lesson 3): A sled sits at the top of a very slick icy slope inclined at 18.0°. Treat the slope as frictionless. Released from rest, what is the sled's acceleration, and how fast is it going after 5.50 s?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝜑= 18.0°, 𝑡= 5.50 s, 𝑣<sub>𝑖</sub>= 0, no friction. Unknown: 𝑎 and 𝑣 after 5.50 s. Physics idea. Along the slope the only force is the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑, so 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 and the mass cancels. Work.

answer.html: 𝑎= 3.03 m/s<sup>2</sup> down the slope; 𝑣= 16.7 m/s after 5.50 s Check. The acceleration is less than 𝑔, as it must be on a shallow slope, and it does not depend on the sled's mass.

items.title: Practice Problem 34 (Lesson 3): A toboggan rider glides at constant speed down a 16.0° slope. What is the coefficient of kinetic friction?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝜑= 16.0°, 𝑎= 0. Unknown: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>. Physics idea. Constant speed means the net force along the slope is zero: 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.

answer.html: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.287 Check. A small angle needs a small coefficient, so a low value is reasonable for snow.

items.title: Practice Problem 35 (Lesson 3): A 28-kg child slides down a playground slide inclined at 38° with 𝜇𝑘= 0.20. What is her acceleration?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 28 kg, 𝜑= 38°, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.20. Unknown: 𝑎. Physics idea. Along the slide: 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Perpendicular: 𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝑎= 𝑔(sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>cos𝜑) = (9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>)(sin38° −0.20 cos38°) = 4.5 m/s<sup>2</sup>

answer.html: 4.5 m/s<sup>2</sup> down the slide Check. It is below the frictionless value 𝑔sin38° = 6.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>, as it should be.

(c) Coefficient of kinetic friction when 𝑎= 0.95 m/s2.

Physics idea. Once sliding, 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= tan𝜑−

answer.html: (c) 𝜇𝑘= 0.36 Check. 𝜇𝑘< 𝜇𝑠 (0.36 < 0.47), as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress 37 (Lesson 3): A 72-kg snowboarder is pulled up an 11.0° slope by a tow rope that exerts 410 N parallel to the slope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.18. What is the snowboarder's acceleration?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 72 kg, 𝑇= 410 N up the slope, 𝜑= 11.0°, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.18. Unknown: 𝑎 (magnitude and direction). Physics idea. Take +𝑥 up the incline. Forces along the slope: tension up; the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 down; kinetic friction 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup> down (the snowboarder moves up, so friction opposes that). Perpendicular: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑= (72)(9.80) sin11.0° = 135 N,
𝑎=

answer.html: 2.1 m/s<sup>2</sup>, directed up the incline Check. Net force ≈151 N and 151 / 72 = 2.1 m/s<sup>2</sup>; positive means speeding up while moving up.

items.title: Check Your Progress 38 (Lesson 3): A wet 18.0-N towel hangs at the middle of a clothesline stretched between two trees; each half of the line sags at an angle of 4.0° below the horizontal. Draw a free-body diagram of the midpoint and find the tension in the line. Why can you never pull a loaded line perfectly tight?

question.html: Physics idea. The midpoint is in equilibrium, so the two tensions together balance the towel's weight. If each half of the line makes an angle 𝛼 with the horizontal, the horizontal components cancel and the vertical components add:
Work.

That is more than 7 times the towel's weight. For a smaller angle the tension gets even larger: 𝛼= 1.0° gives 𝑇≈5.2 × 10<sup>2</sup> N, about 29 times the weight. A perfectly straight line would have 𝛼= 0, which would need an infinite tension to hold any weight.

answer.html: 𝑇= 𝑊/ (2 sin𝛼) = 1.3 × 10<sup>2</sup> N for 𝛼= 4.0°. A line can never be perfectly horizontal under a load because the vertical component of the tension must equal the weight, which would need an infinite tension.

items.title: Check Your Progress 39 (Lesson 3): A banner is hung by eight cables, each with a tension of 950 N. Five of the cables make an angle of 12.0° with the vertical and three make 6.0° with the vertical. What is the mass of the banner?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑇= 950 N each; five cables at 12.0°, three at 6.0°. Unknown: 𝑚. Physics idea. The banner is in equilibrium, so the total upward component of the tensions equals the weight. Horizontal components cancel. Work. 𝑚𝑔= 5𝑇cos12.0° + 3𝑇cos6.0° = 5(950)(0.9781) + 3(950)(0.9945) = 7481 N

answer.html: 7.6 × 10<sup>2</sup> kg ( ≈763 kg) Check. If all eight were vertical they would give 7600 N (776 kg), a bit more, as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress 40 (Lesson 3): An 18.0-N picture can be hung from a nail in two ways. In arrangement A the two wire halves each make 12° with the horizontal (a wide, nearly flat V). In arrangement B they each make 40° with the horizontal (a steeper V). Find the tension in the wire for each arrangement and decide which is less likely to snap.

question.html: Physics idea. The nail pulls up on the wire with a force equal to the picture's weight 𝑊. If each wire half makes an angle 𝛼 with the horizontal, the vertical balance is 2𝑇sin𝛼= 𝑊, so 𝑇= 𝑊/ (2 sin𝛼). Work.
A larger 𝛼 means a larger sin𝛼 and so a smaller tension.

answer.html: 𝑇<sub>𝐴</sub>= 43 N and 𝑇<sub>𝐵</sub>= 14 N. Arrangement B (the steeper V) carries about one third of the tension, so it is less likely to break.

items.title: Check Your Progress 41 (Lesson 3, Critical Thinking): Could a crate slide down a ramp at constant velocity with no one pushing or pulling it? If so, what must be true? Find the coefficient needed for a 20° ramp.

question.html: Physics idea. Constant velocity needs zero net force along the ramp. Going down, the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 points down the slope and kinetic friction 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑 points up the slope, so they can balance. Work. The balance is 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑, so 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= tan𝜑. For 𝜑= 20°:

answer.html: Yes, if the surfaces have 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= tan𝜑. For a 20° ramp that is 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.36. (Going up the ramp, by contrast, both forces point down the slope, so a push would be needed.)

items.title: 3D Thinking: Use a Model to Describe: Draw a labeled diagram showing how friction can be increased by a tree-frog-inspired tire tread and decreased by a lotus-leaf-inspired water-repellent coating.

question.html: Open-ended modeling task, so the answer below is a sample response written here. Increase friction (tree-frog-inspired tread). Draw a tire tread block covered with tiny hexagonal pads separated by narrow channels. Label: "hexagonal pads," "channels drain water," "more contact points on a wet road," "larger friction force 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>." Decrease friction (lotus-leaf-inspired coating). Draw a surface covered with tiny bumps with water drops sitting on top of them. Label: "micro-bumps," "air trapped underneath," "water beads up and rolls off," "less adhesion and drag." Common idea. Both use surface structure on a small scale to change the effective coefficient of friction.

answer.html: A two-panel labeled sketch: (1) hexagonal pads with drainage channels giving more contact on a wet surface, so more friction; (2) a bumpy water-repellent surface where drops roll away, so less friction.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon / CER: Explain Your Reasoning: Why do crews spread sand on an icy road? (Use the data: bare ice 𝜇𝑘= 0.08, sanded ice 𝜇𝑘= 0.35.)

question.html: Sample response written here (the evidence summary in your own Summary Table may differ). Claim (final). Crews spread sand to raise the friction between tires and the road so that cars can speed up, stop, and steer safely. Evidence from this module. (1) 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>: friction depends on the two surfaces and the normal force. (2) The data: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub> rises from 0.08 to 0.35 with sand, more than four times larger. (3) The stopping relation 𝑑= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / (2𝜇𝑔): a car braking from 15 m/s stops in
bare ice but only

<sub>2(0.35)(9.80)</sub> = 33 m on sanded ice. (4) A rolling tire can only get a forward push from static friction, limited to 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>. Reasoning. Bare ice has a very low 𝜇, so the maximum friction force is small. The tires spin when accelerating and slide when braking, and the car needs a huge distance to stop. Sand restores a much higher 𝜇, so traction and braking are reliable. The evidence supports the claim.

answer.html: Sanding the road raises the coefficient of friction (from 0.08 to 0.35), shortening the stopping distance at 15 m/s from about 143 m to about 33 m.

items.title: Data Analysis Lab (Go Further): Who goes down the water slide fastest? A water slide is inclined at 22° and is 55 m long. A 95-kg adult and a 30-kg child ride identical mats. Three friends argue: Rosa says the adult arrives first because she is heavier; Sam says the child arrives first because she is lighter; Tomasz says they arrive together. (1) Sketch the situation. (2) State who is correct. (3) Give evidence and reasoning. 1. Sketch the situation.

question.html: Work. Draw a long incline at 22° above the horizontal, 55 m along the slope. At the top draw the adult (95 kg) and the child (30 kg), each on a mat. For each rider a free-body diagram has weight 𝑚𝑔 (down), normal force 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> (perpendicular to the slope), and kinetic friction 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub> (up the slope). The 𝑥-axis points down the slope.

answer.html: Sketch as described: a 22° incline, 55 m long, with the weight, normal, and friction forces on each rider.

items.title: 2. Claim: who is correct?

question.html: Physics idea. Along the slope, 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑, and the mass cancels:
This does not depend on mass as long as both riders have the same 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub> (same kind of mat and slide) and air resistance is negligible.

answer.html: Tomasz is correct. The adult and the child have the same acceleration and reach the bottom at the same time, so Rosa and Sam are both wrong.

items.title: 3. Evidence and reasoning: justify the claim.

question.html: Work. The time to slide a distance 𝑑= 55 m from rest is 𝑑=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sup>2</sup>𝑎𝑡<sup>2</sup>, so 𝑡= √2𝑑/ 𝑎, which depends only on 𝑎. Illustrative numbers (written here, since no friction coefficient is measured): No friction: 𝑎= 𝑔sin22° = 3.67 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑡= √2(55) / 3.67 = 5.5 s for both. With 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.15: 𝑎= 𝑔(sin22° −0.15 cos22°) = 2.31 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑡= √2(55) / 2.31 = 6.9 s for both. Mass appears in both the gravity term and the friction term (the normal force is proportional to 𝑚), so the heavier adult has more driving force but also exactly proportionally more friction and more mass to accelerate.

answer.html: Because 𝑎= 𝑔(sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>cos𝜑) contains no mass, the time 𝑡= √2𝑑/ 𝑎 is the same for the adult and the child (for example, 5.5 s with no friction or 6.9 s if 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.15). In practice a heavier rider may differ slightly because air resistance and mat friction are not exactly proportional to mass.

items.title: Figure 14 caption question, Compare the vertical component of the up-and-right pull to the weight hanging from the ring.

question.html: Physics idea. The ring is in equilibrium, so the net force is zero in each direction separately. Work. Vertically, the only upward force on the ring is the vertical component of the up-and-right pull. The only downward force is the weight. For 𝐹<sub>𝑛𝑒𝑡</sub><sub>,</sub><sub> 𝑦</sub>= 0 they must balance.

answer.html: The equilibrant has the same magnitude as the resultant but points in the opposite direction, so the resultant plus the equilibrant equals zero.

items.title: Text question (Inclined Planes), How does the component of the girl's weight parallel to the incline change when the slide angle increases?

question.html: Physics idea. The parallel component is 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑, where 𝜑 is the angle of the incline above horizontal. Work. For 0° < 𝜑< 90°, sin𝜑 increases with 𝜑. Examples: sin10° = 0.17, sin30° = 0.50, sin60° = 0.87.

answer.html: It gets larger as the angle increases (zero on a flat surface, equal to the full weight on a vertical wall).

items.title: Get It? (Lesson 3, p. 130), Why choose the x-direction parallel to the slope?

answer.html: The acceleration is along the slope, and the normal and friction forces already lie along the axes (perpendicular and parallel to the surface). Only the weight must be resolved, which makes the algebra simplest.

items.title: Practice Problem 29 (Lesson 3), Free-body diagram of an ant climbing at steady speed up an anthill side inclined 30.0° from vertical.

question.html: Physics idea. Steady speed means zero net force. The surface is 30.0° from vertical, which is 60.0° above horizontal. Three forces act: weight (straight down), normal force (perpendicular to the surface, pointing away from it), and friction (parallel to the surface, pointing up the slope). Because the ant does not slip, the friction is static friction. The weight components along and perpendicular to the surface are 𝑚𝑔sin60.0° and 𝑚𝑔cos60.0°, so 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝑚𝑔sin60.0° and 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos60.0°.

answer.html: The diagram shows 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub> down, 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> perpendicular to the surface, and static friction 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub> up the slope. The sum of the three forces is zero.

items.title: Practice Problem 30 (Lesson 3), 0.44-kg cup on a table tilted 15.0°: components of weight parallel and perpendicular to the table.

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 0.44 kg, 𝜑= 15.0°. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>∥</sub> and 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub><sub>⊥</sub>. Physics idea. Resolve the weight 𝑚𝑔 along and perpendicular to the plane: parallel = 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑, perpendicular = 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.

answer.html: Parallel component 1.1 N (down the slope); perpendicular component 4.2 N (into the table) Check. The parallel part is small and the perpendicular part is nearly all of the 4.31 N, as expected for a small angle.

items.title: Practice Problem 31 (Lesson 3), Fernando (43.0 kg) on a banister at 35.0°: normal force?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 43.0 kg, 𝜑= 35.0°. Unknown: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>. Physics idea. Perpendicular to the banister there is no acceleration, so 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> balances the perpendicular weight component: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.

answer.html: 345 N Check. It is less than his weight (421 N), as always on an incline.

items.title: Practice Problem 32 (Lesson 3, Challenge), At what angle is the parallel component of weight half the perpendicular component?

question.html: Physics idea. Parallel = 𝑚𝑔sin𝜃, perpendicular = 𝑚𝑔cos𝜃. Work.

answer.html: 𝜃= 26.6° Check. At 45° the two are equal, so a smaller angle (26.6°) is right for a parallel part that is smaller.

items.title: Practice Problem 33 (Lesson 3), Crate of Example 5 (562 N, 30.0° incline): acceleration and speed after 4.00 s.

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝐹<sub>𝑔</sub>= 562 N, so 𝑚= 562 / 9.80 = 57.3 kg; 𝜑= 30.0°; 𝑡= 4.00 s. The book gives no friction coefficient for this crate, so we treat the incline as frictionless (stated assumption). Unknown: 𝑎 and 𝑣 after 4.00 s (starting from rest). Physics idea. Along the plane the only force is the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑, so 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 and the mass cancels. Work.

answer.html: 𝑎= 4.90 m/s<sup>2</sup> down the plane; 𝑣= 19.6 m/s after 4.00 s (assuming no friction) Check. 4.90 = 𝑔/ 2 for a 30° slope, a well-known result.

items.title: Practice Problem 34 (Lesson 3), Jorge slides at constant speed on the 27° slide. Coefficient of kinetic friction?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝜑= 27°, 𝑎= 0. Unknown: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>. Physics idea. Constant speed means the net force along the slide is zero: 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>= 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work.

answer.html: 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.51 Check. It is larger than Ichiko's 0.23, which is why Jorge does not accelerate.

items.title: Practice Problem 35 (Lesson 3), Stacie (45 kg) on a 45° slide, 𝜇𝑘= 0.25: acceleration?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 45 kg, 𝜑= 45°, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.25. Unknown: 𝑎. Physics idea. Along the slide: 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Perpendicular: 𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝑎= 𝑔(sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>cos𝜑) = (9.80 m/s<sup>2</sup>)(sin45° −0.25 cos45°) = 5.2 m/s<sup>2</sup>

answer.html: 5.2 m/s<sup>2</sup> down the slide Check. It is below the frictionless value 𝑔sin45° = 6.9 m/s<sup>2</sup>, as it should be.

items.title: Practice Problem 36 (Lesson 3, Challenge), Two physics books; tilt angles 21°, 17°, 21°, 18°, 19° (a) Average 𝜑.

question.html: (b) Coefficient of static friction.
(c) Coefficient of kinetic friction when 𝑎= 1.3 m/s2.

Physics idea. Once sliding, 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= tan𝜑−

answer.html: (c) 𝜇𝑘= 0.21 Check. 𝜇𝑘< 𝜇𝑠 (0.21 < 0.35), as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress 37 (Lesson 3), Water skier (63 kg) pulled up a 14.0° incline by 512 N; 𝜇𝑘= 0.27. Acceleration?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑚= 63 kg, 𝑇= 512 N up the slope, 𝜑= 14.0°, 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.27. Unknown: 𝑎 (magnitude and direction). Physics idea. Take +𝑥 up the incline. Forces along the slope: tension up; the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 down; kinetic friction 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup> down (the skier moves up, so friction opposes that). Perpendicular: 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>= 𝑚𝑔cos𝜑. Work. 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑= (63)(9.80) sin14.0° = 149 N,
𝑎=

answer.html: 3.2 m/s<sup>2</sup>, directed up the incline Check. Net force ≈201 N and 201 / 63 = 3.2 m/s<sup>2</sup>; positive means speeding up while moving up.

items.title: Check Your Progress 38 (Lesson 3), Pulling a stuck car with a rope tied to a tree: draw a free-body diagram and explain why a small force gives a large force on the car.

question.html: Physics idea. Pulling at the midpoint at right angles bends the rope slightly. The midpoint is in equilibrium, so the two tensions together balance your pull. Work. If each half of the rope makes a small angle 𝛼 with the original straight line, the components along the rope direction cancel and the components along your pull add:
For a small 𝛼, sin𝛼 is tiny, so 𝑇 is much larger than 𝐹. For example, 𝛼= 5° gives 𝑇≈5.7𝐹, and 𝛼= 1° gives 𝑇≈29𝐹. The tension is also the force the rope exerts on the car.

answer.html: At the rope's midpoint, the two tensions must balance your sideways pull: 𝑇= 𝐹/ (2 sin𝛼). When the angle 𝛼 is small the tension (and so the force on the car) is many times larger than 𝐹.

items.title: Check Your Progress 39 (Lesson 3), Scoreboard hung by ten cables (six at 8.0°, four at 10.0° from vertical), each 1300 N. Mass?

question.html: What we know / need to find. 𝑇= 1300 N each; six cables at 8.0°, four at 10.0°. Unknown: 𝑚. Physics idea. The scoreboard is in equilibrium, so the total upward component of the tensions equals the weight. Horizontal components cancel in pairs. Work. 𝑚𝑔= 6𝑇cos8.0° + 4𝑇cos10.0° = 6(1300)(0.9903) + 4(1300)(0.9848) = 12 845 N

answer.html: 1.3 × 10<sup>3</sup> kg ( ≈1311 kg) Check. If all ten were vertical they would give 13 000 N (1327 kg), a bit more, as expected.

items.title: Check Your Progress 40 (Lesson 3), Hanging a painting (Figure 20): left (short wire, nearly flat) or right (steeper wire)?

question.html: What we know / need to find. From the figure: on the left the wire makes a small angle with the horizontal (wide angle at the nail); on the right the wire is steeper (narrower angle at the nail). Physics idea. The nail pulls up with a force equal to the painting's weight 𝑚𝑔. If each wire makes an angle 𝛼 with the horizontal, the vertical balance is 2𝑇sin𝛼= 𝑚𝑔, so 𝑇= 𝑚𝑔/ (2 sin𝛼). Work. A larger 𝛼 means a larger sin𝛼 and so a smaller tension. For example, with 𝛼= 15°, 𝑇= 1.93 𝑚𝑔; with 𝛼= 45°, 𝑇= 0.71 𝑚𝑔.

answer.html: Hang it as in the right-hand picture. The steeper wires carry less tension, so they are less likely to break. The nearly flat wires on the left need very large tensions.

items.title: Check Your Progress 41 (Lesson 3, Critical Thinking), Could a child slide up a slide at constant velocity with no push or pull?

question.html: Physics idea. Constant velocity needs zero net force along the slide. Going up, both the weight component 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑 and kinetic friction 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑 point down the slope. With no other force, nothing points up the slope. Work. The balance would be 0 = −𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑, which requires 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= −tan𝜑, a negative value.

answer.html: No. Coefficients of friction are never negative, and both gravity's parallel component and friction point down the slope, so the child would slow down and stop.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Use a Model to Describe, draw a labeled diagram showing how friction can be increased or decreased using biomimetics.

question.html: Open-ended modeling task, so the answer below is a sample response written here. Increase friction (clingfish disc). Draw the rim of the disc as many tiny hair-like structures pressed against a wet surface. Label: "microscopic hairs," "many more contact points," "high points bond temporarily," "larger friction force 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>." Decrease friction (shark skin denticles). Draw overlapping small ridged scales (denticles) with water flowing along the grooves. Label: "denticle ridges," "smooth flow of water," "less drag/friction," "less fuel used." Common idea. Both use surface structure on a small scale to change the effective coefficient of friction.

answer.html: A two-panel labeled sketch: (1) clingfish disc with microscopic hairs giving more contact points, so more friction; (2) shark-skin denticles guiding water flow, so less friction.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon / CER: Explain Your Reasoning, Why is the specialized train washing the tracks?

question.html: Sample response written here (the evidence summary in your own Summary Table may differ). Claim (final). The train washes the tracks to remove slippery contaminants so the wheel-rail friction stays high. Evidence from this module. (1) 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub>= 𝜇𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub>: friction depends on the two surfaces and the normal force. (2) Table 2: steel on steel with a lubricant has 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>= 0.15 compared with 0.78 for dry steel. (3) The stopping examples (Problems 21 and 22) show 𝑑= 𝑣<sup>2</sup> / (2𝜇𝑔), so halving 𝜇 doubles the stopping distance. (4) A wheel can only get a forward push from static friction, limited to 𝜇<sub>𝑠</sub>𝐹<sup>𝑁</sup>. Reasoning. A contaminated rail has a low 𝜇. Then the maximum friction force is small, so the wheels spin when the train accelerates, particularly up a slope (Lesson 3), and the train needs a much longer distance to stop. Washing the rails restores 𝜇, so traction and braking are reliable. The evidence supports the claim.

answer.html: Cleaning the tracks restores a high coefficient of friction, which is needed for the wheels to grip (accelerate and brake) the rails.

items.title: 1. Sketch the situation.

question.html: Work. Draw a long incline at 27° above the horizontal, 70 m along the slope. At the top draw the man (135 kg) and the boy (20 kg), each on a sack. For each person a free-body diagram has weight 𝑚𝑔 (down), normal force 𝐹<sub>𝑁</sub> (perpendicular to the slope), and kinetic friction 𝐹<sub>𝑓</sub> (up the slope). The 𝑥-axis points down the slope.

answer.html: Sketch as described: a 27° incline, 70 m long, with the weight, normal, and friction forces on each rider.

items.title: 2. Claim: who is correct?

question.html: Physics idea. Along the slope, 𝑚𝑎= 𝑚𝑔sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>𝑚𝑔cos𝜑, and the mass cancels:
This does not depend on mass as long as both riders have the same 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub> (same kind of sack and slide) and air resistance is negligible.

answer.html: Kako is correct. The man and the boy have the same acceleration and reach the bottom at the same time, so Margaret Mary's "how much less" is zero, and Doug is wrong.

items.title: 3. Evidence and reasoning: justify the claim.

question.html: Work. The time to slide a distance 𝑑= 70 m from rest is 𝑑=<sub> </sub><sup>1</sup> <sup>2</sup>𝑎𝑡<sup>2</sup>, so 𝑡= √2𝑑/ 𝑎, which depends only on 𝑎. Illustrative numbers (written here, since the book gives no friction coefficient): No friction: 𝑎= 𝑔sin27° = 4.45 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑡= √2(70) / 4.45 = 5.6 s for both. With 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.23 (the value in Example 6): 𝑎= 𝑔(sin27° −0.23 cos27°) = 2.44 m/s<sup>2</sup>, 𝑡= √2(70) / 2.44 = 7.6 s for both. Mass appears in both the gravity term and the friction term (the normal force is proportional to 𝑚), so the heavier man has more driving force but also exactly proportionally more friction and more mass to accelerate.

answer.html: Because 𝑎= 𝑔(sin𝜑−𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>cos𝜑) contains no mass, the time 𝑡= √2𝑑/ 𝑎 is the same for the man and the boy (for example, 5.6 s with no friction or 7.6 s if 𝜇<sub>𝑘</sub>= 0.23). In practice a heavier rider may differ slightly because air resistance and sack friction are not exactly proportional to mass.
